speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXPORTS OF WHEAT AND FLOUR
speechtext:
Can the
Minister of Trade and Commerce give an explanation to the house of the situation regarding Canada's exports of wheat and flour for the first eight months of the present crop year in view of statistics which indicate that Canada's exports are the lowest in a five-year period and that our share of the world's markets continues to decline?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXPORTS OF WHEAT AND FLOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the explanation is that our sales for the first 3J months of this crop year were at a very low level indeed. I made a statement in western Canada indicating that confidence in North American prices had been destroyed and that buyers were holding off their purchases. Along about the middle of November buying commenced and sales at this time are considerably ahead of sales at this time last year. Shipments picked up during the winter months. We had a record movement from the maritime ports and very close to a record movement from Pacific ports in that period. But, as hon. members know, Canada is not well equipped to move export grain when the St. Lawrence

and Hudson bay are closed. All we can do is work to the capacity of our winter ports. I am told that there are boats now waiting for berths on both coast's, and I look for very heavy shipments from our ports during the remainder of this crop year. I can assure my hon. friend that over-all clearances of wheat from Canada during this crop year will be greatly in excess of the record of the past two years.

speakeroldname: Hon. Siuart S. Garson (Minister of Jusiice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend did not give me notice of his question, but like the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) I anticipated that this type of question might be asked and I accordingly made inquiries and would reply as follows.
The general rule is that no information is given out as to whether or not an inquiry is being pursued in a particular industry unless and until a report is made to the minister by the restrictive trade practices commission and duly published. In this particular case, the parties themselves appear to have made public the fact that there is an inquiry and, in any event, it has been made public by the fact that some of the parties have sought an injunction in the supreme court of British Columbia to restrain the inquiry upon the ground that section 4 of the Combines Investigation Act applies and have sought a declaration that it does apply. Section 4 provides that:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to apply to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as such workmen or employees.
If on the facts of this matter section 4 does apply, then, of course, there is no contravention of the Combines Investigation Act.
The purpose of the inquiry, which was commenced as a result of a formal complaint under section 7 of the act, is to ascertain whether fish prices are being fixed and the liberties of fishermen are being interfered with by arrangements amongst persons who

Inquiries of the Ministry are not covered by section 4 or in a manner that is not sanctioned by section 4. There is no intention to interfere in the proper activities of any trade union.
In view of all the circumstances, including particularly the court actions that are pending, I believe that is all I should say for the present time.

I should like to compare the coverage given by the press to the introduction of closure with the coverage given to some of the actions which have taken place in this house and which were more likely to destroy parliament

speechtext:
This is probably one of the most important bills that will come before this house in my lifetime, unless we happen to have the misfortune to be engaged in another war. I believe that the building of this pipe line will do more for Canada in the next 20 years than any other thing we could propose. In making this statement, I should like to substantiate it by quoting a few figures regarding the power shortage which likely is to occur in the province of Ontario and which presently is being felt in the province of Quebec.
Some of my good friends in the province of Quebec tell me that the second thousand kilowatt hours of power in that province, for the first time, costs more today than the first thousand. It has been a standard practice, both in Ontario and in Quebec, to set hydro rates at a certain amount for the first thousand kilowatt hours and at a cheaper rate for the second, and possibly at a still cheaper rate for the third thousand kilowatt hours. In order to conserve power in the province of Quebec, they have now raised the rates on the second thousand. This is a very effective way of saving power in a power-short province.
The province of Ontario has a very similar situation. We have had large increases from our hydraulic power, and also from thermal power, but it would be wise to look at future developments in the province of Ontario. I should like to point out that 25 per cent of
4118	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation the province of Ontario is below 500 feet in elevation. As we know, when we are using qur water energy to develop power, we collect the rain that falls and pass it over elevations and through water wheels to produce electric energy. So, when we have a very flat province such as we have in Ontario, with 25 per cent of this area below 500 feet, 67 per cent of it below 1,000 feet, and 100 per cent of it below 2,000 feet, we have developed at Niagara and various other falls most of the available hydroelectric energy.
When you look at the province of Ontario on a map and see that the great lakes system forms almost one side of that province and that the drop in elevation from the westerly tip of lake Superior to the easterly tip of lake Huron and Georgian bay is only 21 feet, you can see that the production of electric energy from the fall in that length is almost impossible. From lake Huron to lake St. Clair we have a drop of only six feet, and from lake St. Clair to lake Erie we have a drop of three feet. This means that the whole side of the province of Ontario is practically level and that our hydroelectric potential from that part of the province is nil. Then we have in Ontario, between lake Ontario and lake Erie, a drop of 326 feet. This is where we produce most of the hydroelectric energy in the province of Ontario. From lake Ontario down the St. Lawrence- and we are going to develop some hydroelectric energy-there is a fall of 246 feet. We are told that, before the energy which we shall derive from the development of the St. Lawrence seaway is ready to be used, the available electrical energy in the province of Ontario will be consumed.
This pipe line which is going to carry gas from Alberta, and which the province of Alberta is anxious to have used in a useful way, will carry nine times the energy of the hydroelectric development at Niagara falls. It is true that some three times the energy developed at Niagara falls will be siphoned off to the United States. But again I should like to mention the fact that when the hydroelectric energy was developed at Niagara falls, a proportion of that energy had to be supplied to the United States. I recall just a week ago looking at my television set and finding that, as the voltage dropped during that storm, the pictures disappeared but you could still hear the voices. We were watching a program from Buffalo and the announcer said, "Something has happened to our supply of electrical energy but as soon as it is resumed your picture will be returned". This incident indicated to me that Buffalo was receiving energy from the same source as that from which I was receiving


it. In other words, they were receiving power from Niagara falls. So when we ship some gas to the United States, we are doing exactly the same as was done when hydroelectric power was developed years ago at Niagara falls. In order to make that development economical, it was necessary to sell to the market in the United States which was available. Hence this bill has the same principle; we propose to sell 200 million cubic feet of gas to the United States.
This source of power is something that the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec require. We require it for the good reason that our records tell us that there is a total of 5,407,000 horsepower of electrical energy available in the province of Ontario at mean minimum flow. The equipment installed to develop electrical energy in the province of Ontario, is 4,006,668 horsepower. In other words, we are prepared to take advantage of three-quarters of the available power that we can produce from our water resources in the province of Ontario. When the total is used the province of Ontario will be a power-starved province.
We need only look at the situation of the people in the province of Ontario and Quebec in order to see that the people have found jobs and have chosen a place to live where cheap power was available. We have in the north country-and I spent some eight years in Kirkland Lake-an area known as the golden mile. I think possibly God gave more riches to that golden mile in Kirkland Lake than to any other mile in the Dominion of Canada. However, there are only some 23,000 people there. Then we go down to Sudbury, and we see that tremendous asset that Sudbury has in nickel. Yet it has attracted very few people to the area of Sudbury. Then when you go to Noranda, you see the tremendous quantities of copper and other minerals there. Yet the population in those centres that I have spoken about is very small compared with the population in the southern part of Ontario and in those parts of Quebec where power is available. So I want to point out just how necessary it is that we bring to Ontario and Quebec six times the available power which we derive from Niagara falls.
It was not to assist our government that Premier Frost has supported the building of this pipe line. Neither was it to hurt the Conservative party in the federal house that Premier Frost has offered to assist in the building of this line. It is in order to benefit the people of the province of Ontario that he has taken his stand that it is necessary to get on with the job and build this pipe line. I should like to point out to the house,

That fact should indicate to the house and to the people just how important the Liberal members and the government think this bill is when it requires each and every one of them from our province to be in the house.
About the power which we shall derive from the pipe line there is another thing that has not been mentioned in the house and it is one of the reasons why there is some urgency in building this line. Gas is different from electricity. If we build a power plant at some waterfall, the minute that the power is available from the generators you could connect it into the grid system and it would be ready for use. But gas is not one of those types of power. In order to build up a market for gas the individual houses that heat their water with electricity will have installed in them a different type of unit to heat the water. This means that the owners of the present houses, with their electric water heaters, will continue to heat their water in their houses with electrical power. But in the new houses or in the new buildings, when gas is available-because it will be cheaper-you will find those houses and buildings being equipped with gas water heaters and in a great many cases the cook stoves will be gas cook stoves. Hence it is going to take a considerable length of time to take advantage of the power which this gas line is going to supply.
It will not mean a quick change in industry. Many of the electric furnaces in the industries in this country will continue to operate with electrical energy after they have this gas power at their door. But over the years, when their electrical equipment wears out or becomes obsolete, it will be replaced by gas burners. It will take several years for this pipe line to lift the load which hydro is carrying and which in five or six years' time will be too great for hydro to handle unless it is augmented by a source of energy such as this. Hence, Mr. Speaker, there is great urgency that this project should be got on with right away. It is with great respect that I pay a compliment to our Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for the move which he has devised to see that the pipe which is now being formed in the fabricating plants of the steel mills is going to be put to its use in Canada.
It is easy for a person who does not understand the problem to get a wrong impression. It takes about a month to change 67509-261
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation over a rolling mill from rolling shapes for I beams and channels to rolling flat plates and developing it into pipe. If this order at the rolling mills were cancelled so that it was necessary for the plant to change the equipment back, it would take them a month's time before they could change back again, then if the orders were renewed a whole season would be lost. You cannot afford to shut down a rolling mill and change it from rolling one shape to another at the whim of some inexperienced person who does not understand the cost of making such a change. It was, therefore, absolutely essential that if this pipe was going to be used this year some move had to be made to have the plant continue rolling it. Great credit should go to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for this move.

There was no real reason why we should have 25 cycle current, but they started with that and they continued to produce it in every new plant which was built until a few years ago.
If we had had free enterprise in Ontario with two companies developing power, one 25 cycle power and one 60 cycle power, there would have been no 25 cycle power sold in the province. It is very simple to understand why that would be so. A motor using 25 cycle current costs about one-third more than a motor that uses 60 cycle current. If we had had two companies under a free enterprise system, there just would not have been any 25 cycle current sold and the taxpayers of Ontario would not have needed to make an expenditure of some $400 million in Ontario to correct the mistake which the government made in producing 25 cycle current.

It also deals with the same amount of money as was contained in the original resolution. It was proved that his reliable information was most unreliable. But, then, several hon. members came back to the same point. The hon. member for Winnipeg North, who is an accountant, purported to cite figures to show that the rates in the United States would be much lower than the rates in Canada. This afternoon the hon. member for Lambton West said: "Oh, well, let us forget about that; we need not worry about the conditions." He insisted on making comparisons with two different things. There is nothing really mysterious about these various conditions of rates. The same principle applies to electric power, to the communication lines, to the telephones. What the hon. member is saying is that you should take the rate of a telephone call in the United States on Sunday and compare it with a Canadian rate of a telephone call on Monday or another day of the week during office hours.
We all know that the telephone rate is cheaper on holidays and Sundays than it is during business hours. It is even cheaper after six o'clock. To compare one rate with the other without taking these various factors into consideration is just plain ridiculous. And yet the hon. member for Lambton West rose in his place this afternoon and said we should not worry about the different factors; we should just take two rates and compare

them. The point is, there are different factors and different rates, and there are a great many that have to be taken into consideration. They negotiated their contract on a 50 per cent load factor. The other company, the Midwestern, which is the company which will take the gas into the United States, negotiated their contract for 200 million cubic feet on a 95 per cent load factor basis; consequently, you cannot compare the two just on that basis. It is easy to break them down to a common denominator. By taking the 75 per cent load factor and by equalizing pressure, which is also another factor to take into consideration, it is found that over a 20-year period Winnipeg Central will pay an average price of 28-3 cents per thousand cubic feet. Over the same period the average price that would be paid by Midwestern would be 29-3 cents. In other words, the export price to the United States works out at an average of slightly more than one cent per thousand cubic feet higher than the price to Winnipeg.
There should not be too much question of that because, as has been pointed out by previous speakers, we have an act called the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, which is on the statute books of this country. Regulation 9 of this act states in very clear language that no company can take gas and sell it cheaper in the United States than it sells it in Canada under similar conditions. This is clearly set out in regulation 9 of our Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. That act has to be complied with. So far, none of the contracts negotiated in Canada has been higher than in the United States. It should be pointed out, as it was previously, that in the case of the United States company, Winnipeg is on an escalator clause basis; whereas the other one is on a constant rate basis, which means that for the first year the Winnipeg company will pay roughly 2 cents more; but in the second year both will be the same; and in the third year the Winnipeg price will be exactly one cent lower; and the fourth year it will be 3 cents lower, and so on.

Interest was created in the possibilities for gas export at that time and several applications were made to the conservation board of Alberta. In 1949 a natural gas export hearing took place and an application was made by Northwest Natural Gas Company and Alberta Natural Gas Company, both predominantly United States companies. Their application was to take gas to the Pacific northwest of the United States.
In October of the same year the Westcoast Transmission Company applied to take gas from Peace river to Vancouver and on to United States markets. They received their permit from the Alberta board in March, 1952, but they received their permit from the United States to take gas into that country only a few months ago. Let me point out that Mr. McMahon, the president, was not able to complete the financing of this enterprise until the licence was granted by the federal power commission in Washington.
Then we go to February, 1950. At this time Western Pipe Lines Limited, predominantly Canadian, applied for a permit to take gas from Winnipeg to Minnesota. In April of the same year Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, headed by a Canadian, also applied to take gas directly south to Minnesota; however, they withdrew their application and applied for one which would permit them to take gas to the Pacific coast.
In August, 1950, McColl-Frontenac and Union Oil applied to take gas to Montana, as was referred to this afternoon. In September, 1950, Canadian Delhi Oils Limited applied to export to eastern Canada over an all-Canadian route. At this stage, in September, 1950,

But I might say the two corrections which have been made are merely a sample of the many that are needed as far as his speech is concerned, because it was largely composed of fabrications and misrepresentations.
I am one of those who perhaps can look at this matter a little differently from other hon. members who have spoken in this house because, like the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), I am from outside the area it is proposed this pipe line will serve. I rather wish I had a little of the eloquent indignation of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich in order to express my opinion concerning the fact that this is called a trans-Canada pipe line. I shall deal with that later.
I want to say that as far as we who live in the eastern provinces of Canada are concerned, while we will receive absolutely no benefit from the gas in Alberta we look upon that natural resource as we would upon any other natural resource of this country. We want to see it developed in the best manner for the people of the Dominion of Canada.

While we expect no benefit from it, we do not want to see this asset wasted nor do we want to see it cost the people of Canada more than it should.
In past years we have often heard it said that Canadians were the most wasteful people in the world as far as their great natural resources were concerned. Possibly that may have been true because we were a new country, but we have had considerable experience and there should be no recurrence of any great waste nor should there be any great misuse of our natural resources.
There are certain basic principles which I think should govern the development of our natural resources. Perhaps the first is that we as Canadians who are proud of these great assets should control their development. I think that is a great fundamental principle that should apply. The second might be that we should conserve and use our natural resources for the benefit of all the people in so far as that can be done. The third is that these great natural resources are not only for the people now living but should be conserved, developed and preserved for the people who will come after us.
As I said a moment ago, we may have been wasteful in the past in the development of our resources because we have had so many good things given to us. I do not suppose there is a country in the world with such a small population which has been so richly endowed as has the Dominion of Canada. In recent years many of these riches have been discovered in the form of great oil fields, great gas fields, base metal discoveries, uranium and other minerals. Having such a small population it may be that we have not been able to digest these riches as well as we possibly would if we had been a great, rich and heavily populated country.
The matter of closure was brought up again this afternoon. It is not my intention to debate closure except to say that I am sorry indeed that this government, after initiating closure on the first reading of this bill, has decided to initiate it again. Every hon. member, no matter what his constituency, has some interest in this pipe line. It has been called one of the great national developments of Canada, and has been compared with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Why should not hon. members representing constituencies from one end of Canada to the other, whether or not those constituencies are in areas to be served by the pipe line, have an opportunity to express their opinions in this House of Commons?
It is not my intention to develop that argument any further, but I think it is an interesting fact to note that members are sent
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation to the House of Commons to express their opinions on matters and events which come before this house. This is not something having to do with war; this is not something in the form of a great national calamity; this is something which has to do with the future and a few weeks or even months would not make much difference. I submit that the government is unfair to the members of this House of Commons and to the people whom they represent when they do not give hon. members an opportunity to express their views on a question of this kind.
There are bound to be many views. I hope I will be excused if I attempt to indicate briefly this afternoon the views of the people of eastern Canada. We remember when the question of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines was brought before the house in 1951, and we remember the sessions of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. We remember the decisions that were made at that time.
I told my constituents over the radio and individually what were the results of the decisions arrived at in the>
committee. Although my people would get no benefit they were pleased to know that this was to be an all-Canadian pipe line and would not go through the United States. We were guaranteed by the people who were asking for incorporation that it would be an allCanadian pipe line. The people of the eastern provinces agreed 100 per cent. There was no doubt that it was to be an all-Canadian pipe line.
The matter of finances was also discussed in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. What were we guaranteed then? We were guaranteed that the pipe line company would pay 100 per cent of the cost of this line. This also appealed to the people of the eastern Canadian provinces, as I am sure it did also to people in other parts of Canada who would not be able to receive gas from this line. There was no objection to it because it was to be an all-Canadian pipe line to be paid for, not by Canada, not by the people of the eastern provinces, but by this company. That also was satisfactory to our people in 1951.
We were told at that time that it would be under the control of Canadians. Later on we found out that a company known as the Hudson Bay Oil and Gas Company would own 327,000 shares; that another United States-controlled company, Canadian Gulf Oil company, would own 327,000 shares; that Tennessee Gas Transmission Company would own 327,000 shares; that other United States companies would own more shares; that in all about 83 per cent of the shares of this
4134	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation company would be controlled in the United States. Our people did not think so much of that as long as the company was to be under the control of a Canadian directorate or the Canadian people. Mr. F. A. Schultz, vice president of Canadian Delhi Oil Limited of Calgary, one of the prime backers of the proposed company, stated before the committee:
The third consideration was that the project had to be economically feasible. We are satisfied at this stage that the line is entirely feasible.
We were told at that time that it was entirely feasible. As I said a moment ago, representing the people of eastern Canada, we were satisfied with the report of Mr. Shultz, the vice president of this company, that it was feasible. Again we heard nothing about the federal government or the people of Canada having to put up money to pay for the pipe line crossing the terrain of northern Ontario. Whilst the remarks of Mr. Tolmie, the parliamentary agent for the proposed company, and some of his engineers have been put on the record before, I would like just to quote again the statements that were made at that time as to the responsibility of the Canadian government in connection with building across the rugged terrain through northern Ontario.
I might say that at that time this company was applying for incorporation. They were willing and ready to promise anything, and they did promise anything and everything to the members of this House of Commons and the people of Canada. Very few of the things that they promised to the parliament of Canada or to the people have been carried out by them. Mr. Tolmie said:
The relative ruggedness of the terrain between Kenora and Sudbury has given some people the idea that this project is a little bit difficult or even impossible and for that reason we have today the engineer who made the survey on behalf of this company. I think he will be able to give you some enlightening comments on the type of country that these pipe-line builders have met in other countries and that the shield country of Canada is not as formidable as we have been led to believe, largely because of going over it by train and plane.
Then he introduced Mr. Floyd Waterfield of the Pipe Line Engineering Company and the Oklahoma Contracting Corporation. Mr. Waterfield gave the following evidence before the committee:
"So, everything being considered," he told the committee, "that so-called south route as I have referred to it along the (great) lakes provided some quite difficult construction problems-but I have seen worse in our country. In Pennsylvania there are certain sections of that country which are difficult particularly across the Tuscarora mountains and in West Virginia. That is a pipe-liner's hell there. So there is nothing in this pipe-line construction that is insurmountable. It


is just big. Some of it is going to be difficult construction but the average over-all cost comes to a very reasonable and reconcilable figure."
They did not want the Canadian people to pay for it. They themselves were prepared to pay for it at that time. They appealed to the people of this country who will get no benefit, to the people in the far-reaching provinces and other parts of Canada which would get no benefit. We had no objections on the evidence and on the report of this company which came here and sought to obtain incorporation.
So what do we have? First, in 1951 we had the promise that it would be an all-Canadian line. Second, there was no financial difficulty; that this company was willing and prepared -not only willing and prepared but they told us of the finances they could get. They told us in the committee that there was some firm in New York, I think, where they could obtain $250 million for the purpose of financing it. We were told they could get all the finance that was needed. We were told that the northern route, which we all agreed here in this House of Commons was a route we would like to see followed, was not a difficult route and that they would build it across there. They would serve Canada and ask no one to help them. But that was in 1951. After they obtained their incorporation, we began to see just what this company had in its mind.
I am sure that in 1951 they must have appeared before the government with their tongues in their cheeks, and that they also gave evidence before this committee with their tongues in their cheeks, because they no sooner got the incorporation than they began to point out the great difficulties in the construction of a Canadian pipe line. First, they told us that the pipe line would not pay unless some 200 million cubic feet of gas were exported daily to the United States.
As has been said here many times they joined with another company, and a new company was formed in 1954. Then they began to point out the great difficulties of the northern route. They said their company coud not build this route; that unless there was assistance from the Canadian government and from the Ontario government it could not be completed. That was in 1954. Then from 1951 to 1956 we have heard this company complaining that they could not do this and could not do that, and they come back again to the government today. They not only ask them to build over the rough terrain in northern Ontario, but now they tell them they cannot even build from the border of Alberta to the city of Winnipeg.
Has there ever been such a change in the promises of such a corporation in the whole

history of this country? They have climbed today on the backs of the Canadian government; and not only are they on their backs but believe me they have their hands very close to the throats of the Canadian government and Canadian people.
The other day the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), said they had blackmailed the Canadian government into giving them conditions for which they had never asked before. I believe the people of Canada will feel that we have been blackmailed; that this company has taken advantage of the position which it has been allowed to attain, and today they are blackmailing the government and the Canadian people to assist them into doing something that they promised some years ago they could do without any assistance.
I can follow some hon. members in their arguments here when they speak entirely from local and personal points of view. For instance, the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking), in speaking this afternoon, in his argument for the pipe line said that in the city of Guelph their old coal apparatus was outworn and out of date and they had to have a new one. He wanted to see the pipe line put through for this reason. That is a good reason for the city of Guelph, a very fine city for which we all have a high regard because it gave us our hon. leader. But it is not reason enough for the people of Canada, it is not reason enough for the people in my part of the country.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), discussing the city of Winnipeg-and he made so many mistakes that he had to be corrected by other hon. members-said it was a great advantage to the city of Winnipeg. Of course it will be a great advantage to the city of Winnipeg; but we are told that if the pipe line is built through the city of Winnipeg and we do not get the 200 million cubic feet per day of gas going into the United States, the amount of money received from the gas sold in the city of Winnipeg will be only a trickle and that no company could afford to ship gas to the city of Winnipeg unless arrangements were made for the gas to be shipped to the United States.
For over a year, since February, 1955, we have waited for the federal power commission in the United States to grant permission to export gas to the United States. We seem to be no further ahead today than we were then. As a matter of fact, with the antagonistic feelings there are against this Trans-Canada Pipe Line company in the United States, it seems as though that permission may not be granted. So we are in a very poor position as far as this development of our gas pipe line is concerned.
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
As I said, I can understand some of the arguments. I can follow to a certain extent the hon. members of the Social Credit party. They have this great and valuable resource in their own province, and they want to sell it. Naturally any person or organization which has a good article wants to sell it. They think that they are going to sell it more quickly if this matter is hurried through at this time without proper organization or without proper study. I do not think that result follows at all. I am much surprised to see the great confidence which some of their members place in this government, and the great applause they sometimes give in this connection when this pipe line is mentioned. I should like to read what the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Thomas) said the other day. As reported at page 3961 of Hansard the hon. member, speaking of the delay, said this:
It is as a result of their fumbling, bumbling and lack of decision that the present step was made necessary.
He was speaking of the federal government, the federal cabinet, at that time. Then he went on to say this:
We have to realize that because of this fumbling and indecision the government have taken the only action they could have taken under the circumstances. I would not be surprised but what one of the greatest causes of indecision within the government was the attitude of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. I say that because he has attempted all through the years to squash anything that would bring any credit to the Social Credit government of Alberta. It is quite possible that by his arguments he led some of the junior members of the cabinet to go along with him.
We also know that over the years it has been the expressed policy of the Liberal party in the province of Alberta that there will be no export of natural resources. They have opposed the export of coal, the export of oil, the export of gas. Now the whole thing has come down to the present situation. The government has made a mess of things.
Still, with that verdict by the members of the Social Credit party as to a government which they themselves have said has made a mess of this pipe line, they will stand up today and defend the action of that government which, in my opinion, is going to make a bigger mess of it than before.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), as a reason why he wanted to see this pipe line built immediately, said the government or the people of Alberta were losing $50,000 a day. I think that is probably a great exaggeration, but I am not sure. However, I should like to ask him this question. If the Alberta government are losing $50,000 a day, who is responsible for their loss?

It will depend upon what the United States does. My hon. friend knows this. It will depend on whether the federal power commission of the United States grants the permit to sell 200 million cubic feet of gas to the United States. Consideration may go on for a year or it may go on for years. It may never happen. Alberta will still be losing that $50,000 a day, and they can blame their friends across the way for that loss.
I can also understand some individuals- and I am speaking of no particular individual; many of them have been mentioned- connected with this gas industry in Alberta. I know a good many of them myself. I can understand these people being extremely anxious to get this thing pushed forward. They have a personal interest. They have an axe to grind.

speechtext: They want to gain something, probably, on the investments they have. They know that if this company fails-as it very well could-this thing is going to be saddled on the government and the people of Canada. They know that, and they do not think they are taking any great risk as far as that is concerned. I have nothing to say about Ontario. They are interested. Our provinces are not. Ontario is an interested party. They want gas no doubt for northern Ontario. They have already been sucked into this thing. Perhaps they were unwilling, but they had to come in. Now that they are in, it looks to me as though it might be more or less a Hobson's choice for them to carry on.

The people of Canada. An attempt is being made to make them the suckers.
This all leads me to say that I agree with the amendment which was moved the other


day by my friend the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and which suggested that first this matter should go to a committee. A few days or a few weeks more spent in discussion of such a great undertaking for the development of this country of ours is not going to make much difference. Years were taken to build the Canadian Pacific Railway. Sir John A. Macdonald had all sorts of trouble-

There is talk about Algoma Steel going to take gas. Algoma Steel is. going to pay nearly twice as much for their gas as will companies down in the United States. If the federal power commission allow gas to be exported to the United States, Algoma Steel will still pay almost twice as much as do the people down in the United States. We have not heard from Montreal, the great city of Canada. We do not know how much of this gas is going to be sold in Montreal, which is 2,200 miles from the gas fields of Alberta. It is going to cost the city of Montreal about twice as much for their gas as is paid in Winnipeg or in Saskatchewan. Have we any reason to believe that these people in that city of Montreal are going to rush in with open arms to take this gas from the Trans-Canada company? How about the city of Ottawa? We all live here part of .the time. I have not heard nor have I seen it reported in the press of Ottawa that the people, business or anyone else are rushing in and asking that this gas be brought into the city of Ottawa in the immediate future.
These are things which I say should be considered by a committee. These are things which should be known by the people before they go ahead. These are the questions which are being asked and which I feel should be answered. What about the cost of construction? In 1951 an estimate was given. Since then we have heard other estimates. However, the cost of construction is going up all the time.	,

speechtext: That is why we should not wait.

We should know just what it is going to cost. There is another thing we ought to know. We have been told many things which we have found out have not been altogether facts. We ought to know whether there are any other companies which are willing to take on the construction of this pipe line. We ought to know whether there is other pipe available as far as these other companies are concerned. There are many other things that should be considered. The opinion of the eastern provinces, of the province of British Columbia and of the province of Quebec should be known.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is not a trans-Canada or a Canadian pipe-line bill. The province of British Columbia will derive no benefit from it. The province of Quebec will derive very little, if any, benefit from it. They are not clamouring for the gas from this pipe line. The maritime provinces will receive absolutely no benefit from it. These are the things which should be taken into Consideration by any committee examining this matter.
I want to speak for a moment about the situation in the maritime provinces. In 1951 the' maritimes had no criticism of this project, but were pleased and anxious to see that this pipe line was being constructed. Today, when they realize that the government of Canada is willing and ready to lend money to a United States concern to construct a pipe line from Alberta to Winnipeg, and then to help construct the portion in Ontario at a cost of some $160 million, the people of the maritimes want to know why this government could not guarantee the bonds of the province of New Brunswick to permit hydro development in that province when it was so badly needed. That is one question which I think, in fairness to the people of New Brunswick and the people of the maritime provinces, the Prime Minister or someone else should answer in this house.
Not so long ago the Prime Minister referred to the maritime provinces when speaking to the Canadian Labour Congress in the city of Toronto. At that time he pointed out that the rest of Canada felt that there had been certain neglect of the eastern provinces, and he felt that something should be done about it. There should be economic redevelopment in the eastern provinces, and special measures should be taken. He also went on to say, and it sounded very logical and reasonable, that the people of the eastern provinces should state just what they wanted and that would be given careful consideration by the federal government.	_
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
I have sat in this house for 20 years, and I have heard repeatedly from members from the maritime provinces. Time and time again they have told this government what they felt was needed for the development of the maritime provinces. The Prime Minister must know. The Prime Minister has taken part in federal-provincial conferences, and there has not been one provincial government from the maritimes that has not had a long list of things it felt the federal government could do to greatly benefit the people in that area.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, there is a lot the federal government can do to help our people. Those things are well known. In the face of what is happening in this parliament today there is no excuse whatever for this federal government not giving assistance to these little provinces down by the sea which are having such a hard struggle to build up their economy. As I said a moment ago, the government is helping a great United States company which promised the people of Canada and the government that they, without any financial assistance, would build this pipe line. This company must have hundreds of millions of dollars at its disposal today which could be used to build this pipe line without federal government aid. This same government refused aid to the little province of New Brunswick, which is trying to develop hydro facilities in order to process the great natural resources being found there at the present time. I say it is unfair to the people of our province, and that is one angle which should be considered and discussed by this government.
There is another matter which I should like to discuss, but I have not much time. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jut-ras), in what I call a speech full of cheap political claptrap, said we were opposed to United States capital. We welcome United States capital into this country, and we have said so time and time again. What we object to is this. We object to United States capital coming in here, buying up all our natural resources and siphoning them out of the country, because it is a well known fact that when your natural resources are taken out of the country your people leave. What we want is more United States capital. In New Brunswick we do not want our minerals to be shipped out of the country. We want United States capital to come in and build smelters and refineries in that area. That is what we want, and that is what we want for this Dominion of Canada.
I can give you an example of United States capital. They own the great Knob mine in Labrador and have built a railroad, which
4138	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation should have been built by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian people, because that is going to be one of the richest parts of the Dominion of Canada. But they own the mines, the railways and the ships at Seven Islands which take the ore from Canada to the United States to be smelted. Those are the things to which we object, Mr. Speaker, not United States capital coming into this country but United States capital taking most of our natural resources out of this country for the employment of their own people and not for the employment of the people here.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my time is up. This bill should be sent to a committee to be studied; there is no question about that'. If there ever was a case of "heads you win, tails I lose"- which the minister mentioned in reverse the other day-we in the maritimes feel that this is such a case. We want this matter thoroughly discussed in a committee so that every angle can be studied, and so that the people of Canada will know where they are going with relation to this bill.

But in any event I want to make it clear that this mouthful phrase about the great natural resources of this country being sold has been adopted by most of the opposition speakers when they do not know what it means. The bill before the house has to do with the construction of a pipe line. The pipe line, of course, will transport natural gas, and in so far as there is any natural resource concerned in this debate it is with respect to the gas itself, and not the pipe line.
Now, sir, this government and this parliament do not own one cubic inch of natural


gas. We are not dealing with the natural resources when we discuss this bill. That belongs, sir, to the province of Alberta, or rather to those persons in Alberta who have discovered the gas and want to sell it.
Let us consider what we in this parliament are called upon to do; let us go back to the discovery of gas. And may I point out that every hon. member could read with profit the comments made by my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), and what was said by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) with respect to this natural resource of Alberta. Both these hon. gentlemen placed before the house the facts with respect to natural gas and what it would mean to the economy of this country if that natural gas is turned into money.
The other day in his speech the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) tried to suggest that he was rather opposed to this whole business. If I understand the tenor of his remarks, they were to the effect that there was no rush in this; that we could go slowly; that we could leave the gas in the ground for the time being if we wanted to and perhaps it could be dug up by a later generation. In his speech the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich took much the same view, and I was a little surprised because the hon. gentleman is not the kind of man to say, "Now that we have gas in British Columbia we do not care what happens to the rest of the country".
Let me go back to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. May I point out to him that in his party there are some gentlemen who could give him a certain instruction with respect to some of the parables in the Bible. May I draw his attention to the fact that in one particular parable the master did not give the reward to the servant who buried his talents in the ground and left them there. The reward given by the master, Mr. Speaker, was to him who had taken his talents and wisely and prudently used them and returned them to the master with interest.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
In the province of Alberta a great many people and a great many companies have spent a great deal of money to find natural gas and oil. They have been desiring to sell that in the markets of Canada and the United States. This government became involved in this argument, as the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) said, only something over two years ago. It is true that we incorporated pipe-line companies before that but in fact, until the Alberta conservation board decided there was

gas within Alberta for the purposes of export, we were not in a position to do anything about it. But having made that decision through the conservation board, the government of Alberta quite rightly would expect this parliament to take some action in some form to carry out their wishes.
At that point, sir, this government was faced with the decision, are we going to uphold the whole policy of every successive government in Canada since 1907, namely not to permit the export of any energy until Canadian demand had been adequately covered? This government made a decision which every hon. member approved, namely that we would not grant a permit until we had decided that Canadian need and Canadian uses would be adequately protected.
I want it clearly understood that the conservation board of the province of Alberta had given that decision as well. I am not suggesting that because we made that decision they had not also taken the same view. But they said, in the Pincher Creek area, or in that particular area, we shall dedicate for export out of Alberta so many hundred million cubic feet of gas a day, I think something between 500 million and 600 million. At that point the federal government came into the picture for the first time. We have made the decision that we will not permit the export out of Canada of more than 200 million cubic feet a day, and that by way of Emerson down to the midwest states. I have not heard anyone in this house in this debate or in a previous debate say that decision was the wrong one to take. What does it mean, sir?

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: That is one of the things we want to find out about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Oh, yes. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that no one in this debate has quarrelled with our decision that if there are somewhere between 500 million and 600 million cubic feet a day of natural gas available for export out of Alberta the proper proportion to export to the United States at the moment at any rate is 200 million cubic feet. Since we made that decision, sir, it followed that we should also require that the remainder of that amount should be transported to eastern Canada for use along the route and in eastern Canada.
It has always been understood, sir, that we should have an all-Canadian pipe line in the sense that the pipe line would run through Canada. No hon. member of this house, as far as I have been able to find out, except the hon. member for Calgary South, has ever advocated any other course. Well, sir, the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company is a federal incorporation; it has a federal charter because it has to have the
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation right to transport gas across international or, at least, across provincial boundaries.
In case anybody feels that he has got himself confused on this issue, I repeat that our position arises only because of the fact that someone wants to transport gas across provincial or international boundaries. We do not own the gas; we have no control over it except that which I have described. Trans-Canada Pipe Lines then made certain engagements to buy and sell gas; to buy it in the west, transport it and sell it in the east. In the course of doing so they asked permission, or at any rate they made a contract, with a company which had to apply to the federal power commission in Washington to import that 200 million cubic feet a day at Emerson.
At that point hon. members of the Conservative party opposite began to point out and suggest, directly and indirectly, that this government was having its decisions made for it by an agency of a foreign government, and I quote from the Leader of the Opposition on another occasion. He said at page 2171 of Hansard:
This proposal is going to delay the delivery of gas by adopting a method that makes us dependent upon the whims of the federal power commission in Washington.
This government has placed itself in the humiliating and improper position where it is bound to wait until an agency of the government of the United States reaches a decision.
We heard those arguments-

My hon. friends of the C.C.F. party have talked at some length and in glowing terms about public ownership and about the Ontario hydro commission as an outstanding example of its success. No one in Ontario will disagree with them. The Ontario hydro commission is an excellent institution which discharges its duties quite well; but there is no comparison at all in this case with the Ontario hydro commission. If my hon. friends were to go out to the province of Alberta and say to that government,

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation "You should produce this natural gas and you should market it within the confines of the province of Alberta," they would be talking about the same thing they are talking about when they mention the Ontario hydro, which develops power in the province of Ontario and sells it within the province.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company found last year that this government and indeed the government of Ontario as well were insisting that the pipe line go through not the shortest northern Ontario route but a northern Ontario route which is longer than they normally would survey, and the result was they expected the government of Ontario and Canada to contribute in some way to the construction of that line which would be at an extra cost because of its length and direction. We have not subsidized that line, and we are making no subsidy at all in the bill before the house. Let any hon. member opposite who uses the word subsidy correct himself and speak of a loan.
The province of Ontario, desiring to have natural gas in Ontario and desiring to assist this government in providing it in the reasonably near future, entered into an agreement with us that they would help finance that northern Ontario section of the trans-Canada pipe line. That is part of the bill before the house. We are advancing money. We are creating a crown corporation for the purpose of constructing a line and leasing it and perhaps ultimately selling it to the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company. Now I understand, Mr. Speaker, that even this part of our proposal does not meet with the approval of hon. members opposite but let me remind them that the premier of the province of Ontario and his government felt

that this was wise and desirable in the interests of the people of the province of Ontario.
May I just now, sir, by way of interjection, answer what the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) has said. This government and any government of Canada would be hopelessly unable to say on all occasions and on every occasion, "We shall do something for every part of Canada at this particular moment". This government has stayed in office for many reasons, but one of them is that we have given full consideration to the sectional requirements of this country.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: You have not a very good idea of the meaning of requirements.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
It may be, Mr. Speaker, that at any given time there will not be something we can do for a particular part of Canada, but we are in office because when the opportunity arises we have always seized it and we shall do so in the future.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company made its contract with the United States company which wanted to import gas into the United States, that company made an application to the federal power commission for the purpose of obtaining an import permit. I think that consideration began in December-certainly the hearing began in early February-and the hearings are not yet completed but are expected to be completed some time before the summer holidays. This spring, sir, we were faced with a decision to be taken. That decision was, shall we await further a decision of the federal power commission which appears to be necessary before financing can be made available to Trans-Canada, and if we wait what will be the damage, if any, to the Canadian economy in waiting one more year?
Ordinarily a minister of finance is not inclined to loan anyone $80 million, and when this proposal was considered in this department I must say I gave it a certain amount of critical examination. But let us consider the advantages and disadvantages of the proposal to do what this bill now provides for.
This bill provides for the construction of the western leg of this pipe line this year. By the way, sir, something which may be interesting to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is this. I believe he made up the minds of some government supporters when his party two weeks ago today moved the adjournment of this house on a matter of urgent public business, namely the method of financing the western leg. In the course of speaking to that motion and before Your Honour disallowed it the hon. member said

this urgency "relates to getting something done without further delay in western Canada". He said further:
Your Honour realizes that the urgency that confronts us today is that unless some action is taken before long the western leg of the across-Canada pipe line cannot be built this year.
He also went on to say that it would be desirable to give parliament the views of his party "as to what they feel should be done to get this project under way without further delay".
Mr. Speaker, in April this year it became evident that if the federal power commission were not to complete its work immediately this government would be faced with the decision, as I said before, as to whether to delay this project one year or to take some action. At that point it would have been easy to say, "We shall not intervene at all; we shall await the decision of the federal power commission, and if it is successful no doubt this company will be able to finance itself by next season". However, Mr. Speaker, there was another factor that had to be considered.
This company ordered 34-inch pipe last year. That pipe is now partly rolled, and the remainder will be rolled and ready within a matter of days or weeks. But, Mr. Speaker, that involves an investment of between $30 and $40 million and it was highly unlikely, that those who had ordered that pipe would be content to carry the pipe for another season.
Now, if it happened perchance that the federal power commission did not give a decision until late this year it was extremely unlikely-indeed, the odds were very much against it-that we would be able to acquire pipe after that in time for the construction period of 1957, and that the first pipe would be laid for the western leg in July, 1958. Well, sir, that was our choice. We could risk that or we could take the action we are taking here.
I come back, then, to what the hon. member for Lethbridge and my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys have said, that in Alberta there are millions of dollars worth of natural gas capped and blanketed down, of no use whatever to the economy of Canada at the moment. The Minister of Finance is entitled to consider the condition of the economy and the revenues which will come into his coffers should business continue at a high level.
This project; the building of the pipe line itself; the installations in the consumer homes; the installations in industry and the installations in municipal institutions, we thought would run to a cost of something over $1
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation billion spent in the Canadian economy over the next five years. But more than that, sir, if all this wealth is to be tapped and used, may I point out that this government at the present rate, if these companies are successful in selling their gas at a profit, will take 45 per cent of that profit by way of corporation income tax.
When my friend the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich-and perhaps also the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but particularly the former-appeals to the Minister of Finance to go out to Vancouver island and explain to his constituents why a municipal corporation has to go without taxes from us, or why the local hospital should not have a wing on it, all I can say is, "Bless your soul, if this project gets going we will have enough money for all the things you have asked for".

speechtext:
There is another factor in the economic situation of Canada which ought to be considered, and that is the needs of the province of Ontario. In Ontario we have about one-half the industrial production of Canada and about one-third of the population. When I speak now I am speaking as Minister of Finance, but at the same time I cannot help thinking that I represent a portion of that province. The premier of that province has said on more than one occasion that it is extremely difficult for his government to finance the growing expansion of the province. Indeed, some of his criticisms directed at this government with respect to our tax-sharing agreements are simply that the expansion of Ontario has been so great he has not been able to keep pace with it, because every expansion has required some capital outlay.
Let us consider for a moment what that expansion has meant in Ontario. It has meant something to the rural members in this house. When my hon. friends across the way who represent rural ridings speak about lower prices which they claim the farmer is obtaining, let them consider for a moment what

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation would have happened in the past five years if the province of Ontario had not expanded at the rate it has. Everyone from rural Ontario knows that the reason the economy in the rural parts of Ontario is reasonably good at the moment is the growth of the cities and the growth in the number of mouths to be fed in those cities. If we did not have that progress the picture might well be different in rural Ontario, because for one reason or another we are becoming more dependent upon our own consumption of goods than we formerly were.
There was a most interesting debate in the Ontario legislature with respect to this, and I should like to quote the provincial treasurer who spoke as follows on February 21:
The day will soon be upon us when with a continuing growth at the present rate, a shortage of energy resources will set in and progress will accordingly be limited and cut down. It is not only desirable, but is an absolute necessity, that every possible provision be made for access to the people of this province to an abundant supply of natural gas.
I am not going to enter into an argument as to whether prices are adequate or desirable or what they are, because that is a matter of detail with which I am not concerned at the moment. What I am concerned with is that the province of Ontario is, as the provincial treasurer has said, fast coming to the point where sources of energy are becoming fewer and fewer and may possibly dry up. Every member of this house representing an Ontario constituency knows that the Ontario hydro is finding it difficult to look forward and make plans for power for those who need it. Indeed the St. Lawrence waterway, which was expected to provide this additional power, is still a matter of a year and a half or two years from being completed. While I am not prepared to give a precise figure, reading statements made by the provincial people I have come to the conclusion that long before that power is delivered every single part of it will have been spoken for.
If that is so, and even if by making do the province could increase its energy sources somewhat, nevertheless that is not good enough because today there are people in the province of Ontario asking the provincial government when they can have power so they may plan ahead. It is no longer a case of saying, "Well, we think you can have power next week or next month or six months from today." They must know, yet they are being told that their power will not be available until one, two or three years hence.
That is why the premier of Ontario and his government have come to the conclusion

that they are ready to put up $35 million with respect to the northern Ontario leg of this pipe line, and are willing to extend the time under which that arrangement was made so as to provide for the passage of this bill in the house. We can then make a partnership agreement on that basis.
What was the alternative to saying that we would provide this? The alternative was to say that we would not. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, and has repeated it more than once in this house, that he believes the pipe line ought to be begun this year, of course under public ownership. I do not know of an hon. member, except the hon. member for Royal and perhaps one or two others like the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, who does not agree that it is desirable that this pipe line be begun this year.
What are the alternatives offered by the opposition groups in this house? The Leader of the Opposition, speaking on behalf of his party, has said in effect, "Let us send this to a standing committee, we can do that without interfering with the time element of having the pipe line this year." I must say there is no possibility whatever of this bill going to a standing committee and having the examination he has in mind and coming out in time to have this job done by Christmas in western Canada.

I shall be glad to quote it. Before I do so, let me say that if we had been recommending that course, how much would they have talked about the opposition being pro-Canada and the government being anti-Canada. The other day the hon. member

If hon. members opposite do not agree with their colleague, and I am not surprised that they do not, what is the situation at the moment? They have no plan as an alternative to that which is being put forward. They agree with the necessity of this job being started this summer. What they are saying in effect is that the government of Canada should not risk $80 million to do it. Let me point out, however, that this government is not risking very much.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
If this bill passes we will advance 90 per cent of the cost of the western leg. For what reason? In order to be able to deliver gas before winter to the city of Winnipeg, among other things; and to get in one of the two construction years that we always thought would be required for this job. If the house passes the bill the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation will be set up and will be authorized to go forward with its plans in conjunction with the province of Ontario for the purpose of continuing the line down as far as Kapuskasing. The completion of the line from Kapuskasing to Toronto and from Toronto to Montreal may very well be done in the next construction season.
Bear in mind what I have said. If the western leg were started in the summer of 1958 there would be no certainty that the eastern section would be completed by the fall of 1959. What I want to say as a representative from the province of Ontario is that I agree heartily with the premier and government of that province when they say that this would be almost fatal to the progress of this province.
The proposal is that we should advance $80 million to the crown corporation, which in turn will lend it to Trans-Canada for the purpose of getting that pipe laid this summer. When the pipe is laid this summer and the gas comes through to the city of Winnipeg, we shall then have before us the possibility of completing this project next summer. I do not know that this will necessarily occur, but at least it is a possibility.
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Why should we do this? My hon. friend from Royal makes the point that we might think this thing over and that there is no great rush; yet he admits that the people in the province of Alberta want to sell their gas now, and not two or three years from now.
We have not heard anything about the people from the province of Saskatchewan, because they have been rather quiet over there, but they will take the gas any time it comes along. The people of the province of Manitoba, and particularly the people of the city of Winnipeg, not only want the gas but they need it. It should be delivered to them at the earliest possible moment.
The people throughout the northern part of the province of Ontario are going to have a fuel substitute for a fuel they now import from Pennsylvania, and at a low cost; and we shall have a greater mining development, which will mean a greater income to this country.
What about the people of the rest of the province of Ontario? There is not a municipality in Ontario on this route which is not waiting for the gas pipe line to come in order to provide gas for them, and that goes for the route from Kapuskasing to Toronto and from Toronto to Montreal. Of course you can make do, but that is not the way in which the Canadian government and the Canadian people want to conduct their economy. One of the reasons this government, as the hon. member for Provencher has said, is so well thought of abroad is that it is stable and you can count on it. What is more, it goes forward instead of standing still.

speechtext:
In the course of this debate a great many members on this side have inquired of the official opposition why they seem to be disregarding and not speaking of the position taken by the government of the province of Ontario. I do not intend to be offensive when I say what I am about to say. It would be difficult, sir, under the circumstances, for a Conservative government of the province of Ontario to take any position which might embarrass the Conservative party in this house.
