speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. At the outset of this talk I want to advise the house, and

especially the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough), that I have no shares in any oil company; that I am not a spokesman for any oil company, and I have no brief for either Mr. Tanner or Mr. Frank McMahon.
It is not often that I pay tribute to any Liberal speech that has been uttered in this house, but I cannot let this moment pass without saying how glad I am that I happened to be in the house before dinner to hear the straightforward denial made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to all the criticism that has been offered.
I think most of us regret that in the debate thus far there has been so much bitterness over a topic that should have been considered very earnestly, quietly and sanely. I am glad, though, that this rancor seems to have disappeared and that we are taking a saner view of the problem which we are trying to solve by bringing out the pros and cons at this time.
There is another hon. member whom I should like to congratulate on this occasion, namely the hon. member for Calgary South, on his able presentation of so many indisputable facts for our consideration. A few days ago we heard a little about trained seals, but this one particular member seems to be one of those independent sort of people who will not submit to training. He just will not put up with the orders of his leader or possibly his so-called superiors. He does not like the Tory tactics. He believes in facts, not fables, and he is trying to live up to that adjective which the Conservatives have attached to the party name, namely "progressive".
For so doing and for having the courage of his convictions he has risked being disowned by his party that claims to be the last bulwark of personal freedom in this House of Commons. Blind to their own actions, they accuse others of obstructing debate; but I am sure the people of Canada will not be so blind to the action that has been demonstrated here.
Then we have the anti-American campaign which the Conservatives let loose in the hope that it would appeal to the people and form a weapon to spearhead their next federal election battle. I would like to put on record the opinion of the Vernon News, one of the leading papers in my riding, which dealt with this in an editorial on April 26, 1956. I shall not read the whole article, Mr. Speaker. The heading is:
Prosperity depends largely on United States capital in Canada.
The article goes on to say:
The dangerous luxury of belittling the United States, its people, and its objectives has assumed a new form in Canada.
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
The Conservative group in parliament, surprising enough, seems to want to assume the leadership here, in its frantic attempt to grasp any stick that will prove a scourge to the government back.
The Conservatives know as well as anybody that if the flow of United States capital to their country was turned off suddenly, our vaunted prosperity would vanish overnight. Canada simply lacks the money to sustain the gigantic volume of investment required.
It is equally false to imply that we are simply hewers of wood and haulers of water for another's benefit. Statistics show that Canada is building a manufacturing plant for processing its own resources at a rate straining its economic being this year.
Anti-Americanism is at the root of such irresponsible talk as has recently come from some Conservatives in parliament. Hating the United States is a luxury far too rich for the Canadian diet.
To this I say amen. On Friday last reference was made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam to the British Columbia Social Credit members in this house. It is rather difficult to let this pass without notice. I know this hon. gentleman is in the habit of making irresponsible statements both in and out of the house and has embarrassed himself and his party thereby. Perhaps, like the kick from a mule, we should consider where it came from; but when he tries to imply that I show more allegiance to the treasury of the Manning government than to the welfare of the Canadian people he is going just a little too far. It is just another of his irresponsible statements that I am sure he regrets after he has had time to think and the emotional strain of trying to justify his foolishness has worn off.
Then the other day we Social Crediters had another indirect compliment paid to us. I take the remark of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam as an indirect compliment, but we had another compliment paid to us by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I know it was unintentional; nevertheless I would like to express my appreciation. He was referring to another battle that took place in this house last year over the Columbia river, and expressed great surprise over the fact that Liberals and Social Crediters who opposed each other so bitterly at that time are allies here. At this point I believe it was the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) who interjected, "In the same bed".
I would say to the hon. member that we may be in the same bed but we in this corner are not asleep. I will tell the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the people of Canada that we Social Crediters look at each question that comes before us on its own merits. Last year we disagreed with the Liberals on the Columbia river question and we opposed them. Now we believe the

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation Liberal plan for solving the pipe-line question is the best available and we are supporting them. I believe I can go further and say that we bring the same impersonal approach to any national problem that comes up in this house. We are prepared to support any group on any policy that, after careful consideration, we believe is worthy of our support.
In this issue we support the Liberals. That does not mean we have forgotten that our mission in the next federal election is to do our best to unseat them from the throne of government, but we do not believe it is our mission to create issues and try to mislead the Canadian people during this session to find material to work with.
I am glad the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich referred to our action on the Columbia river. What action did the Conservatives and the C.C.F. take then? The same as they are taking today, namely obstruction. What a wonderful record it is to place before the people of Canada at the election they are calling for so loudly at the present time, with their tongues in their cheeks.
Our previous speakers, the hon. members for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), Peace River (Mr. Low), Wetaskiwin (Mr. Thomas) and Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), have done such a noble job in presenting our views on this question that there is little left for me to say. We are concerned about possible regulations being made to assure control of this great project remaining within Canada. It is the duty of this government and every succeeding government not only to assure control of this company but of all business connected with the development of our resources and our industries, and we would ask the government very carefully to consider and try to formulate some plan to assure that at least 51 per cent of the stock of this company remains under Canadian ownership and control.
We hear about the new national policy of an all-Canadian pipe line, Canada first, and so forth. We believe that the people of Canada favour such a policy as this, and Social Crediters for years have endorsed such a policy. In fact, I remember a few years ago we were quite strongly criticized for advocating so vociferously the plan of Canada for Canadians.
In this connection we must admit the present government came out with this policy in connection with the pipe line, possibly with an eye to the 1953 election, at a very embarrassing time for the promoters of Trans-Canada. In negotiations and planning up to that time no such policy was announced by this government. This upset the plans of Trans-Canada, and through this new policy 
the whole problem of financing arose and created the present delay. In order to meet the changed position of the government and construct a line over an uneconomical route, it would not have been any great surprise if the matter of subsidy had entered the picture.
To the honour of the backers of Trans-Canada I will say they did not ask for subsidy; they have merely asked for a loan, although a great many hon. members of this house do not seem to know the difference between a subsidy or a direct grant and a loan. A subsidy would not have been any different from that which was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the construction of another great means of transportation across this country which meant so much in value to the east and the west. But instead of asking for a subsidy they asked for a loan in order to get on with the job more quickly than was possible with the finances they had at their disposal at that time, and in order to build the line to comply with the stipulations laid down by this government.
As I said, we support this national policy, but I believe it should not be a policy which this government may turn on or off in considering individual projects. I am glad to see it so rigidly adhered to in the development and control of our uranium industry. Why is it not applied to our iron ore development? Why do we not have a national policy with regard to iron ore that will build up industries in Canada to process the ore for our own use? Why did we not have a national policy with regard to the St. Lawrence seaway? I would suggest to this government that in all developments and in all projects of national interest the same yardstick of Canada for Canadians should apply. Then we will not have last minute obstacles thrust in the way of development as happened when the new national policy was applied to Trans-Canada.
Now I would like to stress a few points that are directly related to the urgency for immediate action. We have heard a great deal about this matter of urgency; we have some who think the project is not very urgent and of course we have others who believe it is something that should be proceeded with immediately. It is important and it is only right that every phase of this matter should be carefully discussed and the facts-and I stress the word facts-should be presented to the Canadian people. In the debate thus far I am afraid political expediency has been a major consideration in many of the speeches. Now, what are some of the facts?
First there is the urgency that has been stressed by the sponsor of this bill and by

other speakers. I believe there is urgency. This pipe line is a means of distributing a wasting product from Alberta to parts of Canada and the United States where it could be used to advantage. Every day the project is delayed means a loss of $50,000 to Alberta producers. We have heard this laughed at in this house tonight, Mr. Speaker, yet I wonder if that is the way to treat a direct loss which is of such vital concern to the Alberta producers? Perhaps the amount of $50,000 a day does not seem very large, but if we total that sum for a year we have a figure of $18,250,000.
To my mind that is a lot of money; yet that will not be the greatest loss. Householders in eastern Canada are getting tired of shovelling United States coal into their furnaces. Industry is crying for natural gas and promises great expansion when this fuel is available. In this respect I am prepared to accept the words of Premier Frost of Ontario when speaking of this pipe-line deal. I know these words have been quoted many times in this house; nevertheless I am going to quote them again. Premier Frost said:
Time is the very essence of this arrangement and every day's delay invites the most serious consequences to the national economy.
I like that word "national", Mr. Speaker, because it shows that the premier of Ontario is looking beyond the confines of his own province which plays such a vital role in this country of ours.
Agreed on urgency, the question then arises; how to get the line constructed in the least possible time? We have listened to the facts as presented by the minister in introducing the resolution and later the bill. We have made our own investigation and studies of the requirements for prompt action. We have talked with some of the principals involved in the plan and we find this. First, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines has contracts for the purchase and delivery of the pipe necessary for immediate construction of the line. There is an extensive backlog of orders for such pipe, and if not accepted by Trans-Canada it would be immediately sold to others who are clamoring for it and who have unfilled orders waiting.
Second, Trans-Canada has connections and contracts with affiliated and independent producers who are in control of sufficient gas to feed the pipe line the moment it is ready to receive it. Third, Trans-Canada has distribution arrangements planned to take care of the gas as soon as it starts flowing to the eastern outlets. Fourth, Trans-Canada has the right of way, has completed surveys and preliminary planning, and has sufficient capital in cash to finance the 10 per cent of the cost of the western section of the line.

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Knowing these facts, I believe no one will dispute the claim that Trans-Canada is the only company in a position to start work at once and satisfy the urgent demands for early construction of the line. With this established, the matter of the government plan for financing enters the picture. Again I would accept the view expressed by Premier Frost in these words:
That the Howe plan for doing so through the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited deal . . . offers the only possibility of getting the line started this year.
In the matter of financing we hear queer statements, statements that I am afraid are irresponsible and made for the purpose of leaving a false impression in the minds of the Canadian people. Today our people are thinking for themselves and, thank goodness, arrive at their own conclusions regardless of political oratory. The Canadian people know the difference between a loan and a gift. They know that money loaned at a rate of 5 per cent interest and secured by all the assets, contracts and agreements of the party getting the loan is not a gift, and I am sure they will not seriously believe the wild statements of the C.C.F. and Conservative parties about the use of taxpayers' money to subsidize Trans-Canada. It is a hard and fast business deal, and in my estimation the government has driven a hard bargain. In fact I wonder that Trans-Canada would accept a loan under such strict terms. It certainly must have had every confidence that it will be able to meet the debt in full when it falls due in March, 1957.

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
This pipe has been contracted for; this pipe is ready for delivery. This government, under a method that would assure control to Canadians, could assure the construction of this pipe line this year without handing over the benefits of Canadian investment to an organization that is 83 per cent controlled in the United States. That would be democracy in action, and that is what we are asking when we object to closure in this manner.
There will be short speeches tomorrow. Others will have other matters to put forward. I shall at that time continue my remarks but, before I sit down tonight, I hope I may be permitted to draw a similarity between the attitude of this government and that of Oliver Cromwell many years ago. When we hear about the fact that there must be no opposition and no delay, I am reminded of the close of Oliver Cromwell's speech to parliament on January 22, 1655, just 301 years ago. This is Cromwell speaking to parliament. This is the dictator who was an admitted dictator:
I think it my duty-to tell you, that it is not for the profit of these nations, nor fit for the common and public good, for you to continue here any longer, and therefore, I do declare unto you, That I do dissolve this parliament.
That, of course, was a dissolution that was intended to not permit the people of the British Isles at that time to express an opinion, but may I say once again that this government has no mandate to carry out this improper procedure. This government has no mandate to use the Canadian taxpayers' money to finance a venture to the advantage of United States investors. We ask the government to go to the people and let the people say what they want done on this occasion.
Mr. Speaker, I call it ten o'clock. I move the adjournment of the debate.
